explanations.explanation: True, friend. God says, "I dispersed them among the nations, and they were scattered throughout the lands." He adds, "I judged them according to their ways and deeds." I think this one hurts.

This one's actually True, friend. The verse says, "I dispersed them among the nations, and they were scattered throughout the lands." That's God scattering them after He poured out His wrath (Ezekiel 36:18 and 36:19). The verse also says He judged them according to their ways and deeds. I think this one hurts.

explanations.answer: They are the LORD's people yet had to leave His land
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Wherever they went, it was said of them, "These are the people of the LORD, yet they had to leave His land." God says that wherever they went, they profaned His holy name. I think that's a lot to carry around, being the walking headline.

explanations.answer: They are the people who defeated Egypt and Edom
explanations.explanation: Nice try, baker, but the verse doesn't say a word about beating Egypt or Edom. What the nations say is, "These are the people of the LORD, yet they had to leave His land." That's a very different headline from a victory lap. It's about the LORD's people and the land they had to leave.

explanations.answer: They are a people without any god of their own
explanations.explanation: Close to the neighborhood, but not the address, baker. The nations don't say Israel has no god. They say, "These are the people of the LORD, yet they had to leave His land." So they knew whose people these were. That's exactly why it touched God's holy name.

Easy one to pick, baker, but this one's False. God says, "It is not for your sake that I will act, O house of Israel, but for My holy name, which you profaned among the nations to which you went." His message is about His name. Read it slow and you can hear it in the words.

That's right, baker, it's False. God tells the house of Israel, "It is not for your sake that I will act, O house of Israel, but for My holy name, which you profaned among the nations to which you went." So the reason He gives is His holy name. I'd say that's a message worth reading twice.

That's it, baker. God says, "Then the nations will know that I am the LORD, declares the Lord GOD…" He says this will happen when He shows His holiness in Israel before their eyes. The knowing is about Him, not about anybody else.

explanations.answer: That Israel is the greatest nation
explanations.explanation: Good guess for a pep rally, baker, but it's not in the verse. God says the nations will know "…that I am the LORD…" Nothing about Israel ranking first. The spotlight stays on Him.

explanations.answer: That their own idols have power
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite direction, baker. God says the nations will know "…that I am the LORD…" He doesn't say they'll find power in their idols. When God shows His holiness, they come to know Him.

Yes, baker. God says He'll show His holiness "…in you before their eyes." and He's speaking to the house of Israel. So the nations will watch it happen in the very people who profaned His name. That's a front row seat.
Not Edom, baker. God is talking to the house of Israel, and He says He'll show His holiness "…in you before their eyes." The "you" is Israel. The nations are the ones watching.
Not Babylon, baker. Look at who God is speaking to: the house of Israel. When He says He'll show His holiness "…in you before their eyes." the "you" is Israel. The nations get the view.

I get the thought, baker, but it's False. God says, "I will also sprinkle clean water on you, and you will be clean." Notice who is doing the sprinkling. Nobody is handed a scrub brush and told to get busy.

You got it, baker, it's False. God says, "I will also sprinkle clean water on you, and you will be clean. I will cleanse you from all your impurities and all your idols." Count the "I wills." God is the one doing the cleaning.

That's it, baker. God says, "I will cleanse you from all your impurities and all your idols." Earlier He said they defiled the land with their idols (Ezekiel 36:18). So this cleansing reaches the very thing He named back then.

Sounds like a nice sentence, baker, but that's not the word. God says, "I will cleanse you from all your impurities and all your idols." The cleansing is about impurities and idols, and idols were named back in verse 18.

I wish it worked on a pile of dirty mixing bowls, baker, but no. The word is idols. God says, "I will cleanse you from all your impurities and all your idols." It ties right back to verse 18, where idols defiled the land.

explanations.answer: A heart of stone for a heart of flesh
explanations.explanation: Right on, baker. God says, "I will remove your heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh." Stone is hard, and flesh is the living kind of heart. And notice it's God who removes the one and gives the other.

explanations.answer: A heart of iron for a heart of gold
explanations.explanation: That's a good line for a country song, baker, but not what the verse says. God says, "I will remove your heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh." Stone out, flesh in. And God is the one making the swap.

explanations.answer: A heart of fear for a heart of courage
explanations.explanation: That's a sweet swap, baker, but it's not this one. The verse says, "I will remove your heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh." God doesn't name fear or courage here. He names stone and flesh.

explanations.answer: Walk in His laws and keep them carefully
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. God says, "And I will put My Spirit within you and cause you to walk in My statutes and to carefully observe My ordinances." Look at how it starts: He puts His Spirit within them first. Then the walking follows.

explanations.answer: Rule over the nations around them
explanations.explanation: Good guess, baker, but the verse points somewhere else. God says He'll "…cause you to walk in My statutes and to carefully observe My ordinances." Ruling over anybody isn't mentioned. It's about walking in His ways.

explanations.answer: Build Him a new house in Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: That's a big project, baker, but it's not in this verse. God says He'll put His Spirit within them and "…cause you to walk in My statutes and to carefully observe My ordinances." No building plans. It's about how they walk.
True, baker. God says, "you will be My people, and I will be your God." Those words come right after He says they'll live in the land He gave their forefathers. It's a simple line, and it says a lot.

Careful, baker, this one's True. God says, "you will be My people, and I will be your God." He says it right after telling them they'll live in the land He gave their forefathers. There's no twist hiding in it.

You've got the idea, baker. The verse says Israel will "…no longer bear reproach among the nations on account of famine." Reproach is the shame others pile on you. So God's plentiful crops lift that off them.

Not quite, baker. The verse says Israel will "…no longer bear reproach among the nations on account of famine." Reproach is shame, not fear. The nations were looking down on them over the famine, not shaking in their sandals.

Nope, baker, it's the opposite. The verse says Israel will "…no longer bear reproach among the nations on account of famine." Reproach means shame, and nobody envies that. God says plentiful fruit and crops will take it away.

That's the one, baker. God says, "Then you will remember your evil ways and wicked deeds, and you will loathe yourselves for your iniquities and abominations." Loathe is a strong word, and it's the one God uses. Hate fits, because it's how they will feel about themselves.

That would be a plot twist, baker, but no. God says they will "…loathe yourselves for your iniquities and abominations." Loathing is the opposite of praise. They will remember their evil ways and wicked deeds, and they will loathe themselves.

Everybody's got a few excuses ready, baker, but that's not the word here. God says, "…you will loathe yourselves for your iniquities and abominations." No excuses show up in the verse. They remember, and they loathe.

explanations.answer: Ashamed and disgraced for their ways
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. God says, "Be ashamed and disgraced for your ways, O house of Israel!" It comes right after "It is not for your sake that I will act…" I think this is a heavy verse.

explanations.answer: Proud of how far they have come
explanations.explanation: That's a feel-good answer, baker, but the verse says the opposite. God says, "Be ashamed and disgraced for your ways, O house of Israel!" Pride isn't anywhere in it.

explanations.answer: Quiet and patient while they wait
explanations.explanation: Sounds peaceful, baker, but that's not what God says. Right after "It is not for your sake that I will act…" He says, "Be ashamed and disgraced for your ways, O house of Israel!" Nothing in that verse about waiting quietly.

True, baker. God says, "On the day I cleanse you from all your iniquities, I will cause the cities to be resettled and the ruins to be rebuilt." He ties the two together: the cleansing and the rebuilding. And He's the one saying "…I will cause…"

Careful, baker, this one's True. God says, "On the day I cleanse you from all your iniquities, I will cause the cities to be resettled and the ruins to be rebuilt." The day of cleansing is the day He names. Nothing tricky hiding in there.

Yes, baker. The people will say, "This land that was desolate has become like the garden of Eden." Genesis 2:8 says God planted a garden in Eden, in the east. So the desolate land is going to be compared to that garden.
Uzza isn't the name Ezekiel uses, baker. The people say the land has become "…like the garden of Eden." Genesis 2:8 says God planted a garden in Eden, in the east. That's the name to remember.

Gethsemane is a real place, baker. It's where Jesus went to pray (Matthew 26:36), and He was arrested there afterward (Matthew 26:50). But it's not the garden in this verse. The people say the land has become "…like the garden of Eden."
That's it, baker. God says, "Once again I will hear the plea of the house of Israel…" A plea is a request made to Him. And "once again" tells me they've been heard by Him before.
I love a good song, baker, but that's not the word. God says, "Once again I will hear the plea of the house of Israel…" A plea is a request, not a tune. He says He'll hear it.
Not vows, baker. The verse says, "Once again I will hear the plea of the house of Israel…" A plea is a request made to Him. That's the thing He says He'll hear.

Yep, baker. God says, "Like the numerous flocks for sacrifices at Jerusalem during her appointed feasts, so the ruined cities will be filled with flocks of people." At the feasts those flocks were many, and that's the picture He picks. That's a lot of people.

That's a big crowd, baker, but not the picture here. God says, "Like the numerous flocks for sacrifices at Jerusalem during her appointed feasts…" Flocks, not soldiers. And the ruined cities are filled with flocks of people.

Pretty picture, baker, but the verse is about animals, not trees. God says, "Like the numerous flocks for sacrifices at Jerusalem during her appointed feasts…" The cities get filled with flocks of people. That's the comparison He uses.
